282	  on 2026-07-29, `add_repo` ran 270–285s a call, `send_later` 117–390s, `list_triggers` 139–325s,
283	  `delete_trigger` 286–301s, `subscribe_pr_activity` 14–237s. They read like cheap registrations,
284	  so a session issues one, sits through minutes of silence, concludes it hung, and issues it again —
285	  and *the duplicate is the dominant cost*, because the first call had already succeeded:
286	  **#562 (`2026-07-29T1500Z`) — 6 `add_repo` calls, 1121s of that session's 1391s of tool
287	  wall-clock (81%)**, with `HelloWorldFlutterApp` added twice (285s + 271s); **#553
288	  (`2026-07-29T2206Z`) — the same PR check-in `send_later`d 4 times, 1107s of 2028s (55%)**; **#544
289	  (`2026-07-29T1248Z`) — `list_triggers` ×2, `delete_trigger` ×2 on one trigger id, `send_later` ×2:
290	  1854s of 2472s (75%)**, in a session whose real work was 166 tool calls. `AskUserQuestion` shares
291	  the shape — #559's session asked one question twice for 218s + 204s. So: **one call per intent,
292	  ever**, and when what you want is "is it green yet", read the check status directly and merge on
293	  the already-green result rather than buying a notification. Budget these calls before making them:
294	  four of them is most of an hour. And to *read* a public sibling repo, `add_repo` is not the route at
295	  all: it attaches nothing and answers that the session's git proxy already serves anonymous reads —
296	  measured 2026-08-11 (#641), 3m40s before the owner interrupted it plus 40s on the re-issue, against
297	  `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> /workspace/<owner>/<repo>` in ~2s.
298	- **Sync local `main` with `git reset --hard origin/main`, never `git pull` — this repo's session
299	  clones are shallow.** The post-merge sync step of `merge-to-main` is where it bites, and it bit
300	  five separate sessions on 2026-07-29 alone (#548, #551, #537, #559 and the session-end capture of
301	  `73a4db48`). A shallow clone has no common ancestor with the fetched remote, so `git pull` either
302	  demands an explicit strategy or reports the stale local ref as carrying unique commits it does not
303	  have — and the tempting reading, "local `main` has work the remote lacks", is wrong every time:
304	  the session's own work is already *in* `origin/main`, which is why it just merged. #537's session
305	  spent 87s across `git pull`, `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` and log comparisons proving
306	  that from scratch; #559's landed on "git sees no common ancestor" the same way. Nothing of value
307	  is ever on this repo's local `main`, so the sync is unconditional: `git fetch origin main && git
308	  reset --hard origin/main`. (Portable — a promote candidate for `git-github`'s merge procedure,
309	  where "your clone may be shallow" is true of any container-hosted session.)
310	- **The home has no `.claudinite/shared/` mount — machinery paths must accept both roots.** A
311	  consumer runs the vendored engine under `.claudinite/shared/engine/…` with packs under
312	  `.claudinite/(shared|local)/packs/…`; the home *is* the corpus and runs the same code from the
313	  repo root. So a path, regex, or workflow command written to the consumer mount shape works
314	  fleet-wide and fails on exactly this repo — the last place anyone exercises it, so the break
315	  surfaces late. Write the two-root form up front: make the `.claudinite/(shared|local)/` prefix
316	  optional in a pattern, and in a command probe for `.claudinite/shared/` first, falling back to
317	  the repo root.
318	- **Tightening a contract that member-owned files must satisfy has NO carrier — baseline
319	  migrations move paths, not schemas — so it lands as a fleet-wide silent break.** Vendoring
320	  refreshes `.claudinite/shared/` only; a member's `.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/pack.mjs` is
321	  the member's own content, which no converge may edit. And `migrations/` cannot help: its record
322	  is a path relocation (`aliases: [{ canonical, legacy }]`, applied by `applyFileAliases`), so it
323	  has no way to express "the field `rules` is now `worldRules`/`workRules`" or "`ruleRoutingGuidance`
324	  is now required" — exactly what #555 tightened, shipping no record because there was none to
325	  ship. The break is worse than loud: `normalizeManifest` returns `{ ...mod, rules }` with `rules`
326	  rebuilt **only** from the two scoped keys, so a legacy manifest's array is overwritten with `[]`
327	  and **that pack's checks simply stop running** — no error, the pack still loads. Measured on
328	  2026-07-30: **eleven local packs across ten of the thirteen members** had to be rewritten by
329	  hand in one session, and the members' own pack tests asserted `pack.rules` and went red on CI
330	  the moment the manifests moved. So before tightening anything a member's own file must satisfy,
331	  ask what carries it across the fleet; if the answer is "nothing", the change is not ready —
332	  accept the legacy shape in `normalizeManifest` (and say so) until a carrier exists, and never
333	  let a stale declaration degrade to *fewer checks running* rather than a failure.
334	- **A stub is copied once and never re-copied — extend its contract through an *optional* key, and let
335	  the declaration itself trigger the staleness check.** Vendoring refreshes `.claudinite/shared/`, but
336	  `packs/*/stubs/` are artifacts a member copied into its own `.github/` and no converge ever touches
337	  again — so a stub that learns to read a new config key is invisible to every repo still holding the
338	  old copy: the config names the key, the copied action ignores it, the run goes green, and the feature
339	  is silently dead in production. `build_vars` (#729) is the shape to copy. The key is **optional**, so
340	  no existing config is invalidated and no member has to be migrated to stay valid. A
341	  **declared-but-unset** value fails the run rather than exporting `""`, which would reproduce the same
342	  silent death one level down. And `release-workflows` flags exactly the combination that reads the key
343	  and ignores it — a config declaring it against an action or workflow copy predating the exporter — so
344	  the repos that opted in are told to re-copy and nobody else sees a finding. That pairing is the
345	  carrier the entry above asks for: an opt-in contract can ship without one only because declaring it
346	  is itself the signal a check can see.
347	- **A migration record is always the newest code; the engine that executes its result is the
348	  member's, and only as new as its last successful converge.** `migrations/apply.mjs` runs from a
349	  **fresh canon clone**, so every member gets today's record — but the worker that then commits and
350	  pushes it is the member's own **vendored** `.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/baselining/worker.mjs`,
351	  frozen at whatever converge last succeeded. So a record that needs a *new engine capability* to be
352	  deliverable is a **deadlock** on any member that hasn't got it yet: the record fires, the converge
353	  fails, the mount never advances — and the engine fix that would make the record deliverable can
354	  never arrive, because the only thing that could carry it is the converge the record is breaking.
355	  Measured 2026-08-05: `sheepdog-fleet-baseline` materialized `.github/workflows/fleet-baseline.yml`,
356	  which the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` may not push, and wedged `missingbulb/Sheepdog`'s every converge
357	  **twice** — the second time *after* the engine fix (#651) had merged to canon, because Sheepdog was
358	  still running the pre-fix worker. So when a record depends on engine behaviour newer than the record's
359	  own landing date, make `appliesTo` **probe the member's own mount** for that capability and stay
360	  inert until it reads back — self-healing in two cycles, no manual step on any member (#652). Probe by
361	  content, not by version: the baselining stamp covers the whole mount and says nothing about *which*
362	  engine change is in it. And fail **safe** — an unreadable or missing mount file must read as "not
363	  capable", which only ever delays that one record instead of wedging the repo.
364	- **When the owner asks why something failed, lead with the throwing call site — `file:line`, the
365	  function, and which side enforced it.** He is asking for the mechanism, not the sequence; an answer
366	  that narrates the flow correctly but never names the line reads as unanswered, and he will ask again.
367	  Measured 2026-08-05 (#649): "explain why the flow failed" → a correct stage-by-stage narrative →
368	  *"You didn't explain my question from before. What exactly threw the error?"* → `worker.mjs:429`,
369	  `execFileSync` on `git push`, refused **remote-side** on receipt → understood immediately. Three
370	  rounds and ~10 minutes for one fact that fits on one line. The local/remote half matters as much as
371	  the line: it is what says why nothing local — the commit, `migrations/apply.mjs`, the suite, the
372	  sweep — saw it coming.
373	- **This repo's fleet machinery reports success from reaching the end of the code path, not from
374	  the artifact — check the response, and alarm on the stamp.** `deliver()` in
375	  `packs/basics/tasks/baselining/worker.mjs` destructured only `json` from the PR-open POST and
376	  never read `status`, so a 403 (the member's *"Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull
377	  requests"* setting, invisible from inside the Action) put the error body in `pr`, left
378	  `pr.node_id` undefined, skipped the auto-merge arm silently — and the run still logged
379	  `preprocessing basics/baselining: ok`. It compounds because `openMaintenancePull` reuses by open
380	  **PR**, not by branch: a cycle that pushes a branch but fails to open its PR finds nothing to
381	  reuse and mints a fresh one nightly. Measured 2026-07-29/30: **eleven of twelve consumers frozen
382	  on the 2026-07-28 canon ref, 27 orphan `claudinite/maintenance-*` branches, several repos
383	  carrying two for one day** — and every nightly run green throughout. Nothing detected it; the
384	  owner did, by feel ("I feel the situation is bad"). Two habits follow. Read the status of every
385	  API write whose result you then branch on — a body-only destructure turns a refusal into a
386	  plausible object. And judge the fleet by **members' stamps**, never by scheduler run
387	  conclusions: the stamp is the only artifact that moves when baselining actually worked, which is
388	  why a stamp-staleness alarm (#331) is the missing guard and not a nice-to-have.
389	- **A fleet task's target list is enumerated dynamically; the routine's reachable-repo grant is
390	  hand-typed UI config — they drift, and the drift completes rather than fails.** The precondition
391	  builds its member list over `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` (`engine/scheduler/signals/fleet.mjs`, "the one
392	  token that can enumerate every repo the owner owns"), while the executor routine's MCP repo scope
393	  is set by hand in a UI no Action can read — so every member adopted from here on is enumerated by
394	  the precondition and invisible to the executor until someone widens the grant, and the gap only
395	  ever widens. Measured 2026-07-31 on #602: the dispatch named 12 members, the session's grant
396	  listed 10, and `growth-promote` reads members **over the API, never a checkout** — so the run
397	  would have noted two denials, proceeded, and filed a PR reading as a complete 12-member sweep.
398	  That is the worse of the two failure shapes: a routing mismatch stalls visibly (nothing happens,
399	  forever, and you notice), an unreachable target *succeeds wrongly*. So a fleet task must **fail
400	  loudly on a Context target it cannot reach** rather than proceed on a partial list, and adopting a
401	  member is not done until the routine's repo scope names it. No check can catch either half — this
402	  is routine config, not repo content.
403	- **`packs/README.md`'s check tally conflicts on every concurrent check-adding PR — recompute it,
404	  never take a side.** The hand-maintained "Hardcoded conformance checks" count is a repo-wide
405	  aggregate that each PR adding a rule must bump, so two such PRs in flight always collide there,
406	  and a branch that sat overnight collides with whatever landed meanwhile. Both sides of the
407	  conflict are stale the moment a third PR merges, so picking one — or incrementing the higher —
408	  is guessing; `packs-tests/catalog-tally.test.mjs` then goes red and the loop repeats. Derive it
409	  instead: discover the packs and count the active rules (`discoverPacks` +
410	  `run-active-pack-rules.mjs`), write that number, re-run the tally test. Measured 2026-07-31: the
411	  same tally was resolved three times in one day across two sessions (67→68 in #600, then 68→69→70
412	  twice inside #593's merge sequence).
413	  The nastier half of the same tally: a PR that **forgets** the aggregate doesn't conflict at all.
414	  #607 bumped its pack's own row in the catalog table — the *other* hand-maintained number a new
415	  rule must update — and never touched the corpus tally, so it merged clean on a suite that had run
416	  **once**, 12.5 hours earlier against a base that predated #606's own check, and left `main` red
417	  for every PR after it until #608 corrected 68 → 69 as an aside. A conflict at least stops you;
418	  the omission is silent, because a whole-tree aggregate is judged against the merged result and
419	  no branch's CI ever sees that. So a green from before `main` moved is not evidence about
420	  post-merge `main`: re-run the suite against current `main` immediately before merging a
421	  rule-adding PR, and update **both** numbers. (Portable — a promote candidate for `git-github`'s
422	  `merge-to-main`, which today says nothing about merging on a stale green.)
423	- **A worker whose cwd sits inside the tree it deletes takes every child with it — and the death
424	  arrives dressed as a legitimate outcome.** Baselining's prework runs with its cwd *inside the
425	  mount* (`.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/baselining/`), and converge step 2 `rmSync`s that
426	  whole tree before re-copying it. On Linux the worker survives on the unlinked inode and so does
427	  every child it spawns — so `check_the_world` died at `process.cwd()` with `ENOENT … uv_cwd`
428	  **before running a single check**, on every night that actually converged. Nothing looked wrong,
429	  because `escalation()` folded the crash into `checks-could-not-run` (worker.mjs:184) — a real code
430	  that reads as "this mount is too old to have checks". Net effect, fleet-wide and invisible: the
431	  conformance gate had never gated a converged tree, and every converging night burned an agent
432	  escalation on it. Caught live on a Sheepdog run, by nobody's test (#689/#691). Two habits. **Give
433	  every spawned child an explicit `cwd`** — `node([…], env, { cwd: root })` — rather than letting it
434	  inherit a directory its parent is about to delete, and resolve a root that cannot vanish underneath
435	  you (`--root`, then `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, then `cwd`: the order `check_the_world` and
436	  `engine/selftest.mjs` now share; the disagreement between them is the only reason selftest survived
437	  the same dead cwd untouched). And **when a crash and a benign state share one outcome code, the
438	  crash is unobservable** — keep "could not run" distinguishable from "had nothing to run".
439	- **When a member's maintenance PR won't land, read the member before theorizing — `unstable` beside
440	  a green sweep is a *parked* run, not a missing repo setting.** GitHub gates `pull_request` runs on
441	  Actions-pushed branches at `action_required`; a parked run never reports, so the PR reads
442	  `mergeable_state: unstable` and `enablePullRequestAutoMerge` refuses it. Measured 2026-08-07 (#676):
443	  a session read that signature as the members lacking *"Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve
444	  pull requests"* and offered to have the owner flip it across the fleet. The owner's *"Check that
445	  setting. I think you're wrong."* was right, and the two reads that settled it took under a minute —
446	  each member's raw `.claudinite-checks.json` (all eight already said `delivery: auto-merge`) and the
447	  head sha's `pull_request` runs (4 of the last 5 parked `action_required`). The tree already knew:
448	  `baselining/worker.mjs` documents both shapes and the session quoted the wrong one — but this is a
449	  mistake of omission you make *without* opening that file, which is why it belongs here rather than
450	  beside the code. So propose a platform-settings change only as a **conclusion**, never as a
451	  diagnosis, and never on a symptom two API reads resolve. (Sibling of the standing ruling above that
452	  what Claudinite ships must run on the settings a member already has — that one is about what to
453	  *build*, this one about what to *believe*.)
454	- **A canon pack's directory name is kebab-case — lowercase words joined by single hyphens.** The
455	  directory name is the pack's public id: members spell it in `.claudinite-checks.json`, a migration's
456	  `declarePacks` op seeds it, the catalog row and every cross-reference repeat it — so a name in another
457	  casing is renamed later across all of them. Every pack under `packs/` follows it; `grow_with_claudinite`
458	  is the single grandfathered exception (it predates the convention and sits in every member's
459	  declaration, so renaming it would be a fleet migration, not a tidy-up). Nothing stated this until now,
460	  which is how `UserPreferencesStore` shipped in #567 and cost a whole-pack rename to
461	  `claude-code-web-users-support` after the owner asked for *"the appropriate casing for pack names"*.
462	  Name from the **surface** the pack serves, not the first feature you are building for it — that same
463	  rename widened the pack from one store to every Claude-Code-web capability. (Convertible: a check over
464	  `packs/*/pack.mjs` directory names would carry this whole rule, and the fixture is trivial — but any
465	  new rule moves `packs/README.md`'s check tally, which a growth-extract run may not touch. Left for the
466	  weekly prose-to-checks sweep's reviewed PR.)
467	- **"No X should decide this" is a question about whether the decision exists at all — never answer it
468	  by relocating the knob one rung out.** Measured 2026-08-09 (#707): asked to retire the task-level
469	  `session_scope` because *"tasks on Sheepdog have the access to the fleet and they know what they
470	  do"*, the session moved the same choice up to the pack manifest as `sessionScope: 'fleet'` — a new
471	  manifest-vocabulary entry, a resolver module, `discover.mjs` wiring, a rehearsal fixture and tests,
472	  all authored, pushed and then deleted one round later on *"Why do you think you need `sessionScope:
473	  'fleet'`? Who does this help?"*. The reach was already implied by **which repo runs the task** — the
474	  sheepdog enforcer *is* the fleet — so the field only ever protected one structural holdout (the
475	  canon's own curation tasks, whose ordinary executor does not hold the fleet), which is an exception
476	  at that caller, not a knob for everyone. So when a declaration is questioned, first ask **who would
477	  ever set it differently, and why they could not be read off the structure**; a single structural
478	  answer means delete the field and document the exception where it lives. Cousin of the standing "a
479	  pack default stays in the pack — don't ask it at adoption" ruling above: both are about refusing to
480	  materialize a decision nobody actually has to make.
481	- **The home is the last repo to receive its own stub changes — nothing delivers to it.** Every member
482	  gets `engine/scheduler/stubs/claudinite-scheduler.yml` written into `.github/workflows/` by its nightly
483	  converge; the canon has no mount and no converge, so its own copy is hand-maintained and drifts from the
484	  stub it ships. That drift is invisible until it is a permission denial in production: the canon's
485	  workflow sat on `actions: read` while the stub had carried `write` since store-release, so the CI
486	  dispatch POST 403'd and **only** the canon's own fold PR stranded — for ten days (#535, fixed in #704).
487	  Paired tests over the two files are not the safety net you think: one already asserted the
488	  `overrides` input on both and said nothing about `permissions`, so the drift walked straight past it.
489	  So when a change touches the vendored stub, edit the canon's `.github/workflows/` copy in the **same
490	  commit** and diff the two whole files, never just the lines you came for.
491	- **Never combine PRs by pushing one's branch onto the other's base — update the PR you're keeping,
492	  close the other** (owner decision, 2026-08-11). GitHub marks a PR merged the moment its head is
493	  reachable from its base, so the push merges it under your name and shows it merged into a branch
494	  that is itself an open PR's head. A later `state: closed` is a no-op — check the API's `merged`
495	  field before reporting (#754).
496	- **One approved change is one PR.** A dispatch prompt's designated branch routes work, not review:
497	  work that completes or corrects an open PR belongs on that PR's branch. Splitting it gives the owner
498	  two gates for one decision and invites approving half — #739's new pack was approvable while
499	  `basics` still held a rule the pack owned.

=== 631a067 ===
631a067f5a0413e154a0d4c1a66275f18b255af9 Phase 4: retire the last engine note and the held stamp (#785)
* Retire the last engine note, and enforce that none returns

Phase 4's conversion for prework-rename, and with it Phase 1's deferred
validator (#768).

The record's own reasoning is why retiring is right: the note only ever
"carried the guidance through the fleet's next cycles", while the DURABLE
driver is the task-declaration-shape finding, which names the exact rename
and does not age out.

The rollout had already dismantled the channel underneath it, measured on the
canary today: the first update-flow cycle DELETED this record from that
member's mount — the version gate says a repo at engine 2 does not need a
record whose change took effect at 1 — while the update flows never write
`claudinite.updated`, the field that held the stamp for this note. So on a
flipped repo the note was already unreachable; keeping it only held the
stamps of repos still on baselining, for work their own check reports.

With the last one gone, the registry can finally reject an engine record
carrying a note, which is what it could not do while the canon still shipped
two: a validator that rejects the tree it lives in is broken on arrival. It
judges by where the record lives, the same structural classifier the rest of
the scheme uses. A pack record may still carry one — that is where such work
belongs, as its update's apply stage.

The engine-update test that asserted the old refusal now asserts its
consequence instead: a repo at version 0 is servable end to end, which is
exactly what the retirement bought.

Refs #768

* Retire the held stamp: versions decide which notes apply

Phase 4's second box (#768). Note selection moves from the date window to the
version gate — the same `migrationApplies` that decides what a mount fetches
and what a check tolerates, so nothing can now disagree about whether a record
still applies.

The hold goes with it. It existed because the date decided selection: a note
had to keep the stamp back or the next run would deselect it. Version
selection needs no such trick — a record leaves the gap only when the version
carrying its change is installed, and nothing before then can drop it.

Removing it is what makes `claudinite.updated` mean one thing again: when this
repo last converged. Held, it meant that OR "agentic work is outstanding", and
the two are indistinguishable from outside — which is how two healthy members
got called dead this morning, by me, on this session's own evidence. The
canary made it permanent rather than temporary: the update flows never write
that field at all, so a flipped repo's held stamp would have frozen forever.

The agent instructions change with the mechanism: presence in the mount IS the
selection now, because the mount carries exactly the records above the
versions the repo has installed. A record the agent can see is one that still
applies, and there is no stamp to withhold.

Refs #768

---------

Co-authored-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
=== 4a52e08 ===
4a52e08900f30f80568d91b3d3ee1a453f8dfcba Versioned updates: Phase 1 complete, the pack flow, the install, the terminal (#782)
* Gate the engine update on its converged tree, and name the custom lane

The last three Phase 1 boxes of #768.

The gate is the converged mount's own selftest --strict, run from the mount
rather than the canon because the copy under test is the one the member will
live with. It exists because of #555: a content check cannot see its own
machinery break, so a green sweep over a broken mount says nothing. Green
defers to the repo's delivery setting; red ends at needs-human with the PR
open, the same shape every other non-green terminal has. An absent selftest
is red, not green — a mount nothing can vouch for is not a passing one.

force-merge-on-red-ci is a per-invocation argument and is never read from the
repo's declaration, with a test that hands it a declaration asking for it and
asserts it is ignored. A stored default would turn one operator's judgment
about one release into standing policy nobody remembers granting. When used,
the outcome records that it was: an override leaving no trace is
indistinguishable from a gate that passed.

The decision is pure and lives with the flow; the shell that will open and
merge the PR carries the token, not the judgment.

The custom update — the rare engine change that must touch .github/workflows/
— is named in updates/README.md: an explicitly credentialed operation with a
written trail in the release row, for workflow files only. Naming it is the
point, since an unnamed lane is how a workflow exception becomes a general
escape hatch for contract changes that should have waited.

Refs #768

* Retire the drained agentic note, and guard the shrinking holdout

Phase 4's note conversion, pulled forward because #779 turned it into a
precondition: the engine flow admits no agentic stage, so an engine record
carrying a note is a stop for any repo whose gap contains it.

pack-independence's note is retired as drained. Measured against the fleet on
2026-08-12 rather than assumed: ten of the twelve members' stamps read
2026-08-05 or later and the remaining two are private and unreadable
anonymously, so even the most stale readable member is 17 days past this
record's 2026-07-19 landing.

prework-rename's note stays, because the same measurement says it is NOT
drained: ClaudiniteCanary and GoogleCalendarEventCreator were both stamped
2026-08-05, before it landed on 2026-08-06, so neither has ever applied it.

That is also why the registry still cannot throw on an engine record carrying
a note — a validator that rejects the tree it ships in is broken on arrival.
The guard is the holdout set itself, named with its reason and its exit
condition, so a NEW engine note fails the suite while the sanctioned one
stands. The moment the set empties, the test says to replace itself with the
throw.

Refs #768

* Build the pack update flow's deterministic half

Phase 2 of #768. The same shape as the engine flow beside it — replace the
pack's tree wholesale, run its records, stamp its version, gate on the
converged tree's self-test — with the three differences that follow from what
a pack is.

It writes .github/workflows/, which the engine flow may not: the scheduler
workflow's content is a function of the task set, so pack changes are what
rewrite it, and this is the flow whose credential can land it. It announces
the withhold handshake for exactly that reason, which is what retires the
withholding pattern.

It enforces minEngineVersion against the version the TARGET runs, not the one
this canon ships: a member updates engine-first, and reading the canon's
number would check a pack against an engine the repo does not have. A blocked
pack is a terminal naming both numbers, before any write — never a guess, and
never a silent skip.

And it ends by saying whether the agentic apply stage is needed, which is only
when a pack version actually moved: that stage exists because the pack's new
rules meet member-authored content, and a run where nothing moved has no such
content to meet. Dispatching it belongs to the shell that can open a session.

Stamps are written per pack, so a pack this run did not touch keeps the number
it really has, and the engine's own stamp is left alone.

Refs #768

* Install from version zero, and one terminal for every flow

Phase 3's install and Phase 2's uniform terminals (#768), both inert.

An install is the pack flow started from zero, and it runs NO migrations —
not as an optimisation but as a correctness rule (owner decision 9). A record
assumes the shapes its own era produced, and an empty repo is not one of them,
so replaying history onto a fresh install is a hazard rather than merely waste.
It stamps the latest version directly, and it says so through the same version
predicate the other flows fetch by rather than a second code path that could
drift from it — asserted by a test that fails the moment the gate is bypassed.

An install refuses a pack the repo already has a version for. Reinstalling
would stamp the newest version while skipping every record between, which is
how a member ends up claiming a state nothing migrated it into.

Unanswered adoption questions end the run exactly like a red check does: PR
open, needs-human, stop. That is the design being emphatic — interviews are one
instance of the rule, never a rule of their own — and it degrades to async,
which the live-session adoption skill never could.

The terminal itself is one function for every flow, with needs-human outranking
everything and the apply stage outranking a merge: landing the rules before
anything reconciles them with the member's own content would call that
reconciliation optional. A flow that reported success but decided nothing is
not a merge either — an unjudged update is exactly what must never merge
itself.

The apply-stage brief carries the orphaned executor-routine verification, the
one check no Action can make.

Refs #768

* Seed ops: install-time effects the repo owns from then on

Phase 3's remaining mechanism (#768). A pack may declare seedOps — template
and dest pairs a fresh install lays down once, the README pack-badge row's
shape generalised.

The run-once guarantee is STRUCTURAL rather than a flag someone must set:
only the install flow reads the field, so an update has nothing to re-run and
cannot rewrite a repo-owned surface. The assurance is behavioural to match —
a pack update over a seeded, then edited, file leaves it exactly as the repo
left it — rather than a check that asserts the code still reads a certain way.

A dest that already exists is never overwritten, on any install. The file is
the member's from the moment it lands, which is the whole seeded-versus-
converged distinction, and an install that clobbered one would be doing what
the distinction exists to prevent.

The manifest vocabulary widens, so the rehearsal fixture that carries a
consumer-authored manifest carries this key too: the vocabulary is closed, and
a widening is only additive on paper until a member's own manifest is
validated with it.

Refs #768

* The skew guard: exactly one mechanism serves a repo

#768's first risk, and the piece the runner shell needs before it can touch a
member. While baselining and the update flows both exist, two mechanisms
converging one mount would race on the same files — and the loser's write
would look like drift the winner then "repairs", nightly, forever.

The flag is per-repo because the transition is: a member moves when the update
that migrates it says so, not when the canon does. A repo that says nothing is
served by baselining, which is what every member does today — the one
direction a default may point, toward what is already true rather than toward
the new thing.

The default is a reading, not a policy. `servedBy` reports whether the repo
actually declared the value, so the flip is a write an update owes rather than
a state the code interprets forever. An unrecognised value reads as undeclared
and carries what it said: it is the one case where guessing could hand a repo
to the wrong mechanism, so a caller that cares can stop and name it.

"Exactly one" is asserted as a property over every declaration shape rather
than trusted to two predicates that could drift apart.

16d801e536a2802d19f1305e8e05988ce8db7573 Engine 2: local-pack declarations normalize themselves (#781)

7984611f8fafd8bc837225ffde7d83e275d53f77 Versioned updates Phase 1: version-gate migration fetching and tolerance (#778)
Owner decision 7, and the plan's one-change constraint: fetching and
migrationActive() move onto versions in the same commit, because a
version-gated fetch beside a date-windowed tolerance would flag legacy
shapes on repos that simply have not updated yet.

A record now declares the version of its owning flow at which its change
takes effect — which flow that is stays structural, read off where the
record lives, so nothing can declare the wrong one. A record applies while
a repo sits below that number: an up-to-date repo fetches none, a lagging
one fetches exactly its gap however old those records are, which is what
the date window structurally could not express. One predicate
(migrationApplies) answers for both fetching and tolerance, so what a mount
receives and what a check tolerates cannot drift.

A repo whose stamp says nothing about a flow falls back to the landed-date
window — a fresh adoption, a repo that has not converged since versions
existed, and the canon itself, which is nobody's member and carries no
stamp. Unknown is answered as unknown rather than as version zero, which
would make every record apply to everything forever.

The version is read out of the record's source rather than by importing it,
because every caller is synchronous — migrationActive runs inside check
bodies. A test imports every real record and asserts the two readings agree,
so the constraint that buys that (a plain literal on its own line) cannot
rot silently.

* Phase 0: version the engine and the packs, and stamp both on the mount

Scaffolding only — nothing reads these numbers yet. The engine gets a
monotonic integer in engine/version.mjs, which the engine walk already
vendors, so every mount carries the version of the code it holds. Each
canon pack declares `version` and `minEngineVersion`; both are optional in
the manifest spec because a member's local packs are repo-owned and
versionless, and validated for shape only — enforcement is the pack
updater's, which is the only caller that knows the target's engine.

The vendor-set computation returns the versions alongside the file set, so
the writer stamps them in the same pass that lays the files down and the
two can never come from different snapshots. A pack with no version gets no
entry rather than a zero.

Refs #768

* Phase 0: label a dispatch issue with the escalation code that woke it

The code was already in the issue body, which makes it readable and not
countable — aggregating it across a fleet meant fetching and parsing every
dispatch issue. As a label it is a search facet, so "which condition
actually fires" is one query per repo set. That measurement is what sizes
the pack-apply stage's budget before Phase 2 commits to its scope.

The label is minted from the fired code rather than listed in the engine:
the codes belong to the prework worker that raises them, which is a pack,
and the engine may not import one. A malformed code mints nothing — a label
nobody can query is worse than none, and the body still carries it.

Refs #768

* Phase 0: re-home each migration record under the flow that owns it

Records split by owner: an engine contract change lands in
engine/migrations/ beside the machinery, a pack's own change under
packs/<pack>/migrations/. Discovery walks both roots and returns
corpus-relative paths, so no caller has to know which flow raised a record,
and each flow can fetch — later version-range — exactly its own set. A
pack's records ride its vendor walk, so they reach the members declaring
that pack, which is where its checks and its tolerance live; applying is
unchanged, since baselining applies from the fresh canon clone where every
record is present.

migrations/apply.mjs and registry.mjs stay as forwarding entry points.
They are not tidiness: every member invokes the applier BY PATH out of a
canon clone, from its own vendored worker, which is only as new as its last
converge. Deleting the path would fail the apply step of every converge
running an older worker — the converge that would have delivered the newer
one — so the mount never advances and the fix can never arrive. They go in
Phase 5, when no member can still call them.

Refs #768

* Phase 0: repair the references the record move left, and rehearse the widened manifest

Four inbound links pointed at records by their old flat path — sheepdog's
README and RULES at the record it owns (now one directory below them), and
two task-prework docs at the applier.

The manifest-vocabulary widening gets a rehearsal fixture rather than a
migration record: it is additive, so no member needs moving, and what
canon CI cannot otherwise answer is whether a CONSUMER-authored manifest
carrying the new key survives validation — the vocabulary is closed, so
every widening is only additive on paper until a member's own pack.mjs
goes through the loader. `versioned-local` converges green, and goes red
with the schema entries removed.

{"number":492,"title":"Growth dedup: method moves into a pack skill; growth-write-scope gates the capture runs' write surface","body":"Closes #491. Rebased onto current `main`.

## The dedup method moves into a skill

`main` applied #491's split to **extract** (#622: `extract-from-activity` + `extract-from-conversations`) but not to **dedup**, whose `task.md` still carries ~41 lines of method inline. This PR finishes the job: `packs/grow_with_claudinite/skills/growth-dedup/SKILL.md` owns the method — the mounted-canon yardstick, remove/strip/rephrase, the keep-test (says *more*, not merely more specifically), checks-as-coverage, the shrink-only discipline — and the task doc keeps only the unattended framing, delegating with "The method lives in the skill." The skill is also invocable in-session when the owner asks to reconcile local packs against the canon.

The dedup run also gets a pinned title, `Claudinite growth: dedup local packs`, matching extract's.

## `growth-write-scope` gates the capture runs

New blocking work-scope rule on `grow_with_claudinite`. Both capture runs' docs say their whole write surface is the repo's own local packs; nothing enforces it, and both now carry `expected_outcome: 'merged-pr'` — extract always, dedup since #731 — so on default delivery settings no human reviews them before they land. Now, when a branch carries one of those runs' pinned commit titles, **every added, modified, or deleted path must sit under `.claudinite/local/packs/`** (legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted). A capture run improves the repo's **packs** — never the canon it prunes against, never the project's own code.

**The trigger is the two runs' full titles, not the `Claudinite growth:` prefix the lifecycle shares.** The lifecycle's other runs have wider surfaces by design: promote writes the canon under `packs/`+`skills/` (canon-curation's `promote-scope` is its gate), and pack discovery must also write the repo-root `.claudinite-checks.json` declaration that activates the pack it authors. Keying on the prefix would red both — a fixture pins that, and it fails if the trigger is widened back.

Enforcement is at two points:
- **Session Stop hook** (work sweep) — everywhere the pack is active, consumers included.
- **Canon CI, before merge** — a self-gating step on every PR via `.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/growth-scope-gate.mjs` (core CI must not name a specific pack — the barriers rule — so the home's local pack owns the invocation, exactly as `promote-scope` does).

**It catches a real regression.** The merged run `922e059` (`Claudinite growth: extract lessons`) edited `packs/README.md` — the shared canon its task doc forbids it to touch — and landed through a PR no human reviewed. That case is a fixture.

## Supporting changes

- `engine/checks/helpers/work.mjs`: `Work` gains a `deleted` delegate (pure mechanism, like `changedFiles`) so the rule can scope deletions.
- `dedup-prune-integrity`'s `doc` pointer follows the strip discipline into the new skill.
- Pack README: a Skills section, and the Rules table now lists `dedup-prune-integrity` (previously missing) and `growth-write-scope`, with the surface boundary and the sibling runs' own gates spelled out.
- `packs/README.md` corpus tally 86 → 87 (the drift guard requires a rule and its tally to move together).
- **Rehearsal fixture** — `consumer-safe-change` (#595) requires a new blocking rule to ship either a migration record or a fixture proving a consumer still converges green. This rule is genuinely additive (it fires only on branches carrying a capture run's commit), so the fixture is the honest answer: a `growth-member` shape declaring `grow_with_claudinite` plus the local packs its capture runs write.
- Fixtures in `packs-tests/grow_with_claudinite/pack.test.mjs` (red-first): a stray file, a stray deletion, and the `packs/README.md` regression each find; an all-inside run passes (both pack roots, in-surface deletions); promote and discover runs are not gated; ordinary branches are ungated; the title counts only at the commit subject; silent on the default branch.

## Verification

- Full suite as CI runs it: **1481/1481 pass**.
- `check_the_world.mjs`: 0 blocking (36 pre-existing advisories on `main`, untouched).
- `check_the_work.mjs` on this branch: clean.
- See-it-fail: reverting the trigger to the bare prefix reds the sibling-runs fixture, confirming it tests what it claims.

Two things worth pulling out of that PR, because they shape later phases:

**The compatibility entry points are load-bearing, not leftovers.** `migrations/apply.mjs` and `migrations/registry.mjs` stay at the flat path while the records move under their flows. Every member invokes the applier *by path* out of a fresh canon clone — from its own **vendored** worker, which is only as new as its last successful converge. **A pack's records now reach only members that declare that pack** — they ride the pack's vendor walk. That is the split working as intended (the tolerance a record activates is for that pack's own checks, which don't run elsewhere), and it does not change *applying*: baselining applies from the fresh canon clone, where every record is present whatever the member declares, so a `declarePacks` seed still lands on a repo that doesn't carry the pack yet. Phase 2's per-pack version gate inherits this coupling — worth stating explicitly there when it's built.

Verified beyond the suite: a real converge into a scratch member stamps `engineVersion: 1` plus per-pack versions, lands exactly the two in-window records under their new homes, and that mount's own `selftest --strict` and `engine/migrations/apply.mjs` both run clean. `check_the_world`'s advisory list is byte-identical to `origin/main`'s.

Phase 1 is the next landable unit and needs a decision before it starts: an engine **release** has to mean something concrete (a tag? a bump commit? gated on which canary run?), since everything downstream — what the updater clones, what a migration's version range is written against — hangs off that definition.

**Baselining, forced on the same repo** ([run 31640053811](https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]Canary/actions/runs/31640053811)):

- the update flow never writes `updated` — it stamps versions;
- baselining, which is what advanced or released `updated`, no longer runs here.

Fleet-wide rollout done tonight — **the body's "The rollout so far" section is superseded**: it is no longer one repo, it is all of them.

## What was flipped

Every member now declares `maintenance.mechanism: "updates"`. The flip is the one line, committed straight to `main` on each repo (a sparse checkout of `.claudinite-checks.json`, `"mechanism": "updates"` inserted beside `delivery`, nothing else touched).

**Live members (10)** — all were at `631a067` / engine 2 first, so each already held the update task and the standing-down baselining worker in the same mount, i.e. no gap between the two mechanisms:
GoogleCalendarEventCreator, EdFringeNow, TLDR, ShoutsAndWhispers, CrosswordChat, ClaudiniteWebsite, MissingBulbWebsite, VascularColoring, LaughCounter, Sheepdog.

**Dormant members (3)** — EdFringeAllocator, gRatio, HelloWorldFlutterApp. Flipped for completeness, but their mounts are old (`f0b6377` / `426987a`, no `engineVersion`) so the declaration is **inert until they are woken**. The sequence is still safe: their own pre-stand-down baselining worker converges them first, and that same converge delivers the update task, so there is never a cycle where neither mechanism serves them. Unverifiable until someone wakes them.

**ClaudiniteCanary** was already flipped (#55).

## Every live member exercised, forced, one cycle each

Zero `needs-human`. Zero failures.

| Outcome | Members |
| --- | --- |
| PR opened and **merged in-cycle** | LaughCounter #171, GoogleCalendarEventCreator #888, ShoutsAndWhispers #130, ClaudiniteWebsite #153, MissingBulbWebsite #130, VascularColoring #95, EdFringeNow #343 |
| **merge** terminal, auto-merge armed, awaiting the repo's own PR CI | TLDR #246, CrosswordChat #177 |
| Clean no-op — `nothing changed — no branch, no PR` | Sheepdog |

Every run reported `engine — ok` then `packs — ok`, both gated on the converged tree's self-test. The repos with no `pull_request` CI merged directly (`no pull_request-triggered workflow — the delivered PR has no checks to wait for`); the ones with CI armed auto-merge and EdFringeNow's landed at 23:31 when its checks went green. The typical diff was 2 files / 84 deletions — the version gate dropping migration records the member no longer needs, same shape as the canary's first cycle.

Sheepdog's no-op is worth calling out as the mechanism working rather than nothing happening: it had converged fully at 22:57, so the update flows found nothing above what it had installed and correctly declined to open a PR. Under baselining that same night would have produced a dated converge PR.

## One finding, filed as #786

The update flows never write `claudinite.ref` or `claudinite.updated` — by design, since stamping a date every cycle is what made baselining noisy. But `fleet-freshness` measures liveness by the **age of the stamped ref**, so on a flipped repo that measure freezes. With one canary that was a curiosity; with the whole fleet migrated it means the sweep will eventually report every healthy member as drifting. Not urgent — it needs canon to move past `631a067` and the age threshold to elapse — but it should be fixed before that happens. #786 has the detail and a suggested shape (branch on the mechanism; judge `updates` repos by version comparison, which is exact rather than estimated).

## What this unblocks

Phase 5's gate was "fleet-wide adoption". That is now met for every non-dormant member. It is **not** met for the three dormant repos, and the risk noted in the body still stands: deleting `packs/basics/tasks/baselining/` while they hold old mounts would strand them, because baselining is the only mechanism their vendored worker can run. They need to be woken and converged before Phase 5 removes it — or Phase 5 needs to accept that they get repaired by hand when they wake.

Closing the loop on the two members my previous comment left mid-CI. **All ten live members are converged and landed** — the rollout is complete, not merely dispatched.

TLDR and CrosswordChat both needed a second cycle, and what happened in between is worth recording because it is a defect rather than a delay:

- Cycle 1 opened PR #246 (TLDR) / #177 (CrosswordChat) on the **merge** terminal. Neither could land in-cycle — their `pull_request` check is parked at `action_required` by the bot-PR approval gate, and the check the worker dispatched instead went green about ten seconds *after* the worker gave up waiting. The log promised `leaving it open for the next run to dispose of`.
- Cycle 2 did not dispose of it. It re-ran the flows against a `main` that was still unconverged (because the first PR never merged), found work, and opened a **fresh** PR — #247 / #178 — which it merged in-cycle at 23:35.
- Net: both repos are correctly converged, and both were left with an orphaned duplicate PR whose diff was already in `main`. I closed #246 and #177 by hand.

Filed as #787. The root cause is that the runner's `nothing changed — no branch, no PR` early return happens *before* anything looks at open update PRs, so no cycle can ever keep that promise: a quiet cycle returns too early, and a busy cycle opens a competitor instead of landing the incumbent. Suggested fix is to dispose of any open `claudinite/update-*` PR before converging — land it if its head sha now has a green run, close it if its diff is already in `main`.

This is litter rather than breakage, but it recurs every cycle on any member whose PR checks are approval-gated, so it is worth fixing before the fleet runs unattended for a stretch.

{"number":788,"title":"sheepdog: merge fleet-census and fleet-freshness into one roster sweep","body":"## The problem

`fleet-census` (daily) and `fleet-freshness` (weekly) walk the same fleet and classify the same
repos, twice, from two independently-maintained pieces of code.

Both do their own `paged(gh, '/user/repos?affiliation=owner')`, their own owner filter, their own
"enumeration returned no repos" guard, their own home/canon/archived/fork/excluded structural
skips, and their own `readDeclaration` per repo. The freshness sweep's header says it "takes
coverage as given" — but it cannot actually take it, because the census's verdict lives in another
process on another cadence, so it re-derives the whole thing. `check-fleet-coverage.mjs:172` and
`check-fleet-freshness.mjs:341` are the same eight lines with different error strings.

That duplication has already produced divergence in the classification itself:

- **`exclude` is applied at different points.** The census tests `optOut` only after finding a repo
  *uncovered* (`check-fleet-coverage.mjs:198`), so an excluded repo that still carries a declaration
  is reported **covered**. The freshness sweep tests `exclude` *before* reading anything
  (`check-fleet-freshness.mjs:355`), so the same repo is **out of scope**. Both are defensible; that
  they were decided separately is the problem.
- **`unknown` means different things.** A declaration that will not parse fails the census run. A
  compare call that 500s fails the freshness run. Neither knows the other happened, so an operator
  reading one green run and one red one cannot tell which half of the fleet picture is trustworthy.

## The change

One task, `fleet-roster`, replacing both. One enumeration, one declaration read per repo, one
roster; two finding families consuming it, each keeping its own semantics.

- `tasks/fleet-roster/check-fleet-roster.mjs` — config, canon branch, enumeration, and the single
  per-repo classification pass.
- `tasks/fleet-roster/adoption-issues.mjs` — the `fleet-adoption` label, bodies, convergence and
  the coverage section of the report. Lifted from `check-fleet-coverage.mjs` unchanged.
- `tasks/fleet-roster/drift-issues.mjs` — the `fleet-drift` label, `classifyFreshness`, the
  per-member probe, convergence and the freshness section. Lifted from
  `check-fleet-freshness.mjs` unchanged.

The two issue label families stay distinct, so every open `fleet-adoption` and `fleet-drift` thread
converges exactly as it does today. Both existing report renderers are kept verbatim and printed as
two sections of one summary.

### Cadence: daily, and this costs API calls rather than saving them

Worth stating plainly, because "two walks become one" suggests a saving that is not there. Today
the census reads one declaration per repo daily; freshness adds two reads per covered member once a
week. Merged and run daily, the freshness probe runs daily too — roughly two extra REST reads per
covered member on the six days that were previously census-only. On a fleet this size that is a
couple of hundred extra reads a week against a 5000/hour limit.

What is bought for it: drift converges within a day of appearing instead of within a week, and the
alternative — a daily task hand-rolling a weekly gate for half its body — would reimplement dueness,
which is stateless in the engine (a slot is due iff its time falls in `(last successful run, now]`)
and not something a task can ask about from inside itself.

The real wins are structural: one roster instead of two that can disagree, one report, one failure
boundary, and the duplicated enumerate-and-classify code deleted.

### One behaviour change, deliberate

Splitting `unknown` by family. A declaration that cannot be read is unknown to **both** halves (it
is the input both share). A probe failure — scheduler read, canon compare — is unknown to the
**freshness** half only; the coverage half already read that repo's declaration successfully and
still classifies it. The run fails if either family has an unknown, so nothing is downgraded to
silence. Today a compare failure makes the repo invisible to freshness while the census, in its
separate run, reports it fine and nothing connects the two.

### Out of scope

- **#786** — that `fleet-freshness` judges by stamped `ref` age, which the update flows never
  refresh. `classifyFreshness` moves file unchanged; the bug moves with it and is still #786's.
- The other merges considered alongside this one (`fleet-baseline` + `fleet-add-missing-packs` as
  one dispatcher; `fleet-pack-seeds` folded into `fleet-add-missing-packs`) — separate calls,
  neither taken here.

## Migration

`fleet-census` and `fleet-freshness` are removed. Both are `agent_model: 'none'`, so neither has
outstanding dispatch issues; the engine already records a vanished task as `task-gone`, and run
records are log lines rather than state keyed by id. The pack is declared only by the enforcer repo,
whose `sheepdog` config carries no per-task keys — `parseSheepdogConfig` reads
`{ owner, kind, exclude, canonRepo, staleDays, packSeeds }` and none of them names a task. So no
baseline migration record is needed: the next converge vendors the new task and drops the two old
ones.

{"number":787,"title":"An update PR that cannot land in-cycle is superseded, not disposed of — the next cycle opens a duplicate","body":"Observed live on TLDR and CrosswordChat while migrating the fleet onto the update mechanism (#768). Both recovered on their own, so this is litter rather than breakage — but it is litter that recurs on every cycle for any member whose PR checks are approval-gated.

## What happens

`engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs` (via the update runner) says what it intends when it cannot land a delivered PR in its own cycle:

```
main requires nothing to merge — skipping the doomed auto-merge arm; waiting for this run's 1 dispatched run(s) and landing PR #246 here
PR #246 not landable this run (no successful run on its head sha) — leaving it open for the next run to dispose of
```

The next run does not dispose of it. It re-runs the flows against a `main` that is still unconverged — precisely because the previous PR never merged — finds work to do, and opens a **new** PR with the same content:

```
merged PR #247 in-cycle — its pull_request run is parked at action_required (never ran) while the dispatched run passed
```

So `main` converges, but the earlier PR is left open forever with a diff that is now already merged. On TLDR that was #246 (superseded by #247); on CrosswordChat, #177 (superseded by #178). Both closed by hand.

## Why the first cycle failed to land

The `pull_request`-triggered check never runs — it is parked at `action_required` by GitHub's approval requirement for bot-authored PRs. The worker correctly detects this and dispatches an equivalent run via `workflow_dispatch` instead, but then gives up on the wait roughly ten seconds before that run reports green. So the failure is a race in the wait, not a broken gate. Widening the wait would fix these two cases and not the general one.

## The actual defect

The promise "leaving it open for the next run to dispose of" has no implementing code path. The runner's early return is:

```js
const changed = git(['-C', root, 'status', '--porcelain']).trim();
if (!changed && terminal.action !== 'needs-human') {
  console.log('update: nothing changed — no branch, no PR');
  return;
}
```

A cycle that finds nothing to do returns *before* looking at open update PRs — so the only cycle that could dispose of a stranded PR is one that has its own work to deliver, and that cycle opens a competing PR instead of landing the old one. Either branch of the condition drops it.

## Suggested shape

Before the converge, have the runner look for an open PR on a `claudinite/update-*` branch and dispose of it first: land it if its head sha now has a successful run, close it if its diff is already in `main`. That makes the sentence in the log true, keeps at most one update PR alive per member, and is the same "dispose of the previous delivery" step baselining effectively gets for free by re-deriving its branch name per day.

Worth deciding at the same time whether the wait should tolerate a check that goes green seconds later, since that is what turned a one-cycle delay into a duplicate here.

## Related

- #768 — the fleet migration that surfaced it.
- #786 — the other finding from the same rollout (`fleet-freshness` measures by a `ref` the update flows never write). Independent bug.
- Member-side note, not a Claudinite bug: TLDR's `test-extension.yml`, `test-requirements.yml` and `test-server.yml` run on `pull_request` with no `workflow_dispatch:` trigger, so delivery cannot start them at all — the worker logged this explicitly for each.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/issues/787","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-12T23:37:43Z","updated_at":"2026-08-12T23:37:43Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":786,"title":"fleet-freshness judges by stamped `ref` age, which the update flows never refresh","body":"Found while migrating the fleet onto `maintenance.mechanism: "updates"` (#768). Not urgent tonight — it starts biting once canon moves past `631a067` and the sweep's age threshold elapses — but it now applies to **every** member rather than one canary.

## The mismatch

`packs/sheepdog/tasks/fleet-freshness/check-fleet-freshness.mjs` takes the age of `claudinite.ref` as the liveness measure, and says so explicitly:

> `claudinite.updated` advances only when canon actually changed that member's vendor set. Age of the STAMPED REF is therefore the honest liveness measure

That was true under baselining, where `vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs` writes `{updated, ref, engineVersion, packVersions}` on every converge. The update flows write neither `updated` nor `ref`:

- `updates/engine-update.mjs` → `next.claudinite = { ...next.claudinite, engineVersion: ENGINE_VERSION }`
- `updates/pack-update.mjs` and `updates/install.mjs` → the same, for `packVersions`

So on a repo served by `updates`, `ref` freezes at whatever baselining last wrote. As canon advances, the freshness sweep will report healthy, fully-current members as increasingly behind, and open `fleet-drift` issues for them — with no signal distinguishing them from a genuinely wedged repo.

## Why "just write `ref` every cycle" is the wrong fix

A no-op update cycle currently produces *no PR at all* — Sheepdog tonight: `update: nothing changed — no branch, no PR`. Stamping a fresh `ref`/`updated` on every converge would put a changed file in every cycle on every member, resurrecting exactly the daily-noise problem the versioned scheme removed. The date-based measure is also strictly weaker than what the member now carries: `engineVersion` and `packVersions` answer "is this current?" exactly, where a date only estimates it.

## Suggested shape

Teach the sweep to branch on the mechanism it already can read from the declaration (`engine/served-by.mjs` is vendored into the enforcer's mount):

- **`baselining`** — unchanged: age of the stamped `ref`.
- **`updates`** — compare `engineVersion` against canon's `ENGINE_VERSION`, and each entry of `packVersions` against that pack's manifest `version`. Behind ⇒ drift, with the gap named. This makes `behind` exact and lets the issue body say *which* version is missing.

The enforcer already fetches canon to resolve the stamped ref against the default branch, so the inputs are in hand.

Open question for the owner, and the reason this is an issue rather than a PR: whether `ref` should still be maintained under `updates` as a debugging fact (which canon commit this mount came from), written only when the converge actually changed files. That keeps no-op cycles silent while preserving provenance — it was `ref` that made tonight's diagnosis possible. It is not needed for the freshness measure above.

## Related

- #768 — the migration; the whole fleet is now on `updates`, which is what makes this fleet-wide.
- missingbulb/Sheepdog#172 — `fleet-baseline` reports `failed: 0` because it counts dispatches, not outcomes. Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/prose-to-checks

# Convert existing prose to checks

A completeness-critic over a repo's own packs: prose that is always-testable but was never converted
becomes a check, so the packs keep shedding context over time instead of only at the moment a rule is
first learned.

## Two callers, differing only in scope

- **The upgrade pass**, as the last step of a
  [growth-extract](../../tasks/growth-extract/task.md) run: the scope is the prose **that run just
  wrote**. Extraction already descends the promotion ladder per lesson, but a lesson written as prose
  under time pressure is exactly where a convertible rule hides, so it gets asked once more before the
  PR opens. Never widen from here into the standing backlog.
- **The weekly [prose-to-checks-sweep](../../tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)**: the scope is the
  **standing backlog** — everything under the pack paths configured for this repo, which the task
  passes in its Context. A consuming repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) by
  default — projects don't improve core canon packs — while **Claudinite itself** also sweeps its core
  `packs/`. Read the prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them).

Plus on demand, when someone asks. Either way: never edit a read-only mounted canon pack under
`.claudinite/shared/`. Everything below is identical for both callers.

## First gate — a working rule, not a product statement

Before asking whether a rule is *testable*, ask whether it belongs to a pack at all: **does it govern
how we work, or state what the product does?** A pack — canon or local — homes the conventions,
gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks whatever the feature happens to be. A rule
asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or that a feature's parts are wired to
each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable spec and the suite that proves
it (the full rule lives in
[generate-project-instructions](../generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md)).

This gate comes **first** because product statements sail through the check-the-world test below —
"this module must export `X`" has an obvious static signature. Converting one splits a feature's
definition across two systems and lands half of it in the one no test of the product ever reads.
Load-bearingness is not the test: a real gap in product coverage is a *requirements* gap. Neither is build
quality — a product statement converts into a genuinely well-made check, clean parse and see-it-fail proof and
all, and is still the wrong kind. The discriminator, applied **before** you write anything: *if the product
changed its mind tomorrow, would this rule be wrong?* Wrong → it's a requirement, and a red check would report
a product decision as a process violation. Still true whatever the product decides → it's a working rule.

A product statement already sitting in pack prose is mis-homed, and a sweep is not the place to
re-home it. **Leave the prose and log it** as a mis-homed rule, the same way an un-checkable
candidate is logged — never cement it as a check.

## What to look for — the check-the-world test

For each rule that cleared the gate, ask the one question from
[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**

- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.

**"Already covered by another check" is a claim to test, not to reason out** — hand the sibling check a file
that violates the rule before dropping the candidate as a duplicate. A ban list only covers the routes whoever
wrote it thought of, so the routes it misses are invisible to exactly the reasoning that drew it: three sweeps
running dropped an "the app opens no socket" rule because a neighbouring check banned the obvious networking
import, while the base library re-exported a raw socket call that sailed straight through.

**"Not statically checkable" is a verdict about the tree's shape when it was taken, not about the rule —
re-derive it against today's sources.** A removal, a migration or a consolidation can collapse the entry points
a rule had to cover, and the objection dies with them: a "one deletable storage directory" rule needed
data-flow tracing while many entry points wrote paths, and needed none once one root remained. So when a sweep
meets prose an earlier sweep left behind, re-ask the question rather than trusting the recorded answer. (This
covers the *technical* verdict only — an owner's rejection of a conversion is settled.)

**Read the conversion tracker's prior comments before authoring, not after.** Independent re-derivation is
exactly how duplicate work happens: a fresh reading of the same prose will happily re-nominate a rule, build it
out in full, and only then discover it was built and rejected before. The tracker is a precondition of the
work, not a place to log it — and record each rejection with its reason so the next run can act on it.

**A static signature is necessary, not sufficient.** Both shapes the working-discipline rules bar
— a rule that pins today's code in place, and one derivable from the product's requirements —
answer *yes* here, so screen every candidate against that bar before converting it. Leave either
where it is; routing a requirement to the spec and its suite is its own change, not this sweep's.

The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.

## How to convert one

Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:

> **The upgrade-pass caller lands inside growth-extract's own PR**, which auto-merges after CI — so the
> see-it-fail fixture is the only gate a converted check gets there. Convert only what you can prove;
> anything shakier stays prose and waits for the weekly sweep's reviewed PR.

1. **Author the check** in the owning pack (`<pack>/<rule>.mjs`, listed in its `pack.mjs`) — the
   failure message *is* the rule (what / why / fix / `doc:` pointer back to the prose).
2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
   doesn't ship.
3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory when the rule is
   directional by kind, or when the condition is blocking-grade but **irreversible by the time it is
   observable** (an append-only transcript, a published artifact). A blocking finding no edit can
   retract never converges — it spends every remaining Stop cycle on something nothing can fix.
   Advisory there is *diagnostic*: it names the cause the moment it appears.
   - **Prefer a positive allowlist over an enumerated list of the bad cases.** Match the one allowed
     shape and flag everything else, rather than banning the violations you can name. An allowlist
     catches a variant that doesn't exist yet the day it lands, and turns an indirection (a value
     passed through a variable instead of written literally) into a finding too — refusing to reason
     about indirection is the feature. Invert only where the allowed set is genuinely open-ended.
4. **Delete the prose the check now covers** — whole, never trimmed. The deletion test below is
   how you decide which paragraphs those are.

**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
check to the same fixture bar.

**When a rule mandates a *form*, the check asserts that form — never the intent behind it.** Where
the prose says *write it exactly like this*, the check's whole job is deciding whether the artifact
is that form; inferring what the author meant is unbounded in the wrong direction and leaves the
likeliest reproduction uncaught, since a hand-picked marker list always misses the phrasing nobody
enumerated. Expect a form check to fire on something that breaks the form while causing no harm —
that's the rule as written doing its job, not a reason to re-add intent-guessing.

When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.

## Coming out: the deletion test

Coming out of a conversion, apply the **deletion test**: prose a mechanism fully covers is
deleted, never trimmed. Ask it of every paragraph standing beside a landed check — *with this
paragraph gone, would the check still catch every violation it describes **and** tell the agent
how to fix it?* If yes, it is redundant: delete it whole. The check's failure message is where
the rule lives now and its header comment is where the rationale lives, so a paragraph restating
either pays twice and is the drift trap waiting to spring.

Before concluding prose is the only carrier, look at the pack's **skills** too — an
activity-scoped skill often already holds the map a rule is repeating. Keep only what no artifact
carries.

The test **discriminates** rather than just deleting: a paragraph stays whole whenever it carries
something the check does not — a second rule in the same breath, an exemption the check can't
encode, a value the check can't judge, or a remedy the finding's own `fix` line never states
(a finding renders `what` / `why` / `fix` / `doc`, never the rule's `description`, so a remedy
that lives only in the description is not carried). Two worked calls: an `npm test` invariant
went entirely — the check caught it and the testing-guide skill already listed the suites —
while an `extension-test/` mirror bullet stayed, because the check beside it enforced only the
`package.json` list's sync with the tree and never the mirror convention itself.

Whether a check covers a rule is a judgment about meaning, so this test is applied by a
**reader**, not mechanized.

## Bounds

- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — the deletion test is only ever asked of a rule a
  *landed* check now enforces.
- Run the suite and the sweep green before the PR goes up, and never push to `main` directly. The
  sweep opens its own PR for the owner's approval; the upgrade pass adds its conversion to the
  growth-extract PR already being opened, and opens none of its own.

input.body:
Growth-extract's daily capture, dispatched by #793, over exactly the window named in its Context section.

## Activity half

Read the 12 substantive commits, the merged/touched PRs and the touched issues in the window — almost entirely the versioned-updates rollout (#768 and its phases). Most of what those commits do is already-settled, already-tested implementation (the shape a check or test already pins), which the `extract-from-activity` skill's own bar excludes from becoming a pack lesson.

One genuinely new, durable lesson cleared the bar: **a fleet member's held `claudinite.updated` stamp is indistinguishable from a genuinely stale one unless `ref` is also read.** `heldStamp()` deliberately pins `updated` to the day before a repo's earliest pending agentic note, so a repo converging normally every night can still show a week-old `updated` for as long as that note stays unapplied. This was misread live on 2026-08-12 (#768's own thread): a session called ClaudiniteCanary and GoogleCalendarEventCreator stale on `updated` alone when both were converging hourly. Landed as a canon-specific-gotcha bullet in `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md`.

## Conversation half

Fresh pass over the recent window on `origin/conversation-logs` (the sessions behind #768, #770, #774, #777, #491, and the issue-0 session). The friction present there (repeated `AskUserQuestion` confirmations the owner rejected outright, a stop-hook trip on a missing `Comment class:` line) either resolves to the owner's own working-style preference — explicitly excluded from becoming a pack rule by `extracting-lessons.md` — or is already fully captured by the commits/design docs the same sessions produced. Nothing new cleared the bar here.

## Upgrade pass

Ran `prose-to-checks` over the one new bullet. It governs how to read *another* repo's stamp during an investigation, not a static signature in this repo's own tree, so it stays prose — no check authored.

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`: 1539/1539 pass.
- `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs`: 0 blocking, 35 advisory (pre-existing, unchanged).
- Whole diff is one file under `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md`.

Refs #793
